entry: South Slavic language, the primary language of [[Serbia]], [[Croatia]], [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], and [[Montenegro]]. Serbo-Croatian is a pluricentric language with four mutually intelligible standard varieties: Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, and Montenegrin. Its standardization was initiated in the mid-19th-century Vienna Literary Agreement, decades before a Yugoslav state was established. In the 20th century it served as the lingua franca of [[Yugoslavia]], where it was the official language of four of the six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic. It can be written in the [[Latin script|Latin]] or [[Cyrillic script|Cyrillic]] alphabet, and its orthography is highly phonemic. The breakup of Yugoslavia divided its linguistic identity along ethnic and political lines. Bosnian has since been established as an official standard in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and efforts to codify a separate Montenegrin standard continue. Its grammar, evolved from Common Slavic, preserves seven grammatical cases in nouns, pronouns, and adjectives.

American professional [[Tennis|tennis]] player. Williams turned professional in 1995 and won her first major singles title at the 1999 US Open. She won 73 WTA Tour singles titles, including 23 major singles titles, the most in the Open Era. She was ranked world No. 1 for 319 weeks and finished the year at No. 1 five times. From the 2002 French Open to the 2003 Australian Open she won four consecutive major singles titles, a non-calendar year [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]] nicknamed the "Serena Slam", and she achieved a second Serena Slam in 2014–2015. With her sister Venus she won 14 major women's doubles championships and was undefeated in major doubles finals. Williams won four Olympic gold medals, three in women's doubles. In 2020 the Tennis Channel ranked her the greatest women's tennis player of all time.

National park in northern [[Tanzania]], covering 14,763 sq km (5,700 sq mi). It was established in 1940 and granted strict protection in 1948. The park is known for the largest annual animal migration in the world, of over 1.5 million western white-bearded wildebeest and 250,000 Grant's zebra, along with between 400–500,000 Thomson's gazelle. It is home to the largest [[Lion|lion]] population in Africa. In 1959 an area of 8,300 sq km was split off as the [[Ngorongoro Conservation Area]] to accommodate Maasai land use. The eastern black rhinoceros population was reduced to about 10 individuals in the 1980s by poaching, and fewer than 70 survive in the park. The park is threatened by [[Deforestation|deforestation]], population growth, poaching, and ranching.

Condition of debt bondage and the status of many peasants under [[Feudalism|feudalism]]. Unlike [[Slavery|slaves]], serfs could not be bought or sold individually, though they could be sold together with the land. In return for protection, justice, and the right to cultivate plots for their subsistence, serfs worked the lord's fields and were required to labor in his mines and forests and to maintain roads. Serfdom developed during [[Late antiquity|late antiquity]] and the [[Middle Ages|Early Middle Ages]] and lasted in some countries until the mid-19th century. The decline of serfdom in Western Europe has sometimes been attributed to the [[Black Death]], which reached Europe in 1347. Serfdom grew stronger in Central and Eastern Europe, a development known as "second serfdom". [[Prussia]] abolished it in 1807, and Russia in 1861. The 1956 United Nations Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery prohibits serfdom as a practice similar to slavery.

French singer-songwriter, actor, composer, and director, born Lucien Ginsburg. Regarded as one of the most important figures in French pop, he drew on [[Jazz|jazz]], chanson, and yé-yé early in his career, and later on rock, zouk, [[Funk|funk]], [[Reggae|reggae]], and electronica. He wrote over 550 songs, which have been covered more than 1,000 times. His lyrics used wordplay with humorous, sexual, satirical, or subversive overtones, and his provocative releases caused uproar in [[France]], dividing public opinion. His singles "Je t'aime... moi non plus" and "Bonnie and Clyde" charted in the United Kingdom and Belgium, respectively. After his death he became one of France's best-loved public figures.

Soviet film director, screenwriter, editor, and film theorist. Considered one of the greatest filmmakers of all time, he was a pioneer of montage. His [[Silent film|silent films]] include *Strike* (1925), *Battleship Potemkin* (1925), and *October* (1928). His historical epics include *Alexander Nevsky* (1938) and *Ivan the Terrible* (1945/1958). In 1918 he joined the [[Red Army]] during the [[Russian Civil War]]. He began his career as a theorist in 1923 with "The Montage of Attractions" for the art journal LEF. *Sight and Sound* ranked *Battleship Potemkin* 54th in its decennial poll of the greatest films. His focus on structural issues such as camera angles and crowd movements drew criticism from the Soviet film community, and he was forced to issue public self-criticism and conform his work to the doctrines of socialist realism.

Soviet rocket engineer and spacecraft designer who led the development of the Soviet space program in the early years of the [[Space Race]]. He directed development of the R-7, the world's first [[Intercontinental ballistic missile|intercontinental ballistic missile]]. Under his leadership the Soviet Union launched [[Sputnik 1]], the first artificial satellite, and [[Laika]], the first animal to orbit Earth. His missions carried [[Yuri Gagarin]] into space aboard [[Vostok 1]], the first human in space, and enabled Alexei Leonov's spacewalk during Voskhod 2. Arrested in 1938 during the [[Great Purge]] on charges later shown to be false, he spent nearly six years in prison and labor camps. During his lifetime he was publicly identified only as "chief designer," partly to protect him from assassination, and his name was disclosed only after his death.

Russian composer, pianist, and conductor, active in the [[Soviet Union]]. Regarded as one of the major composers of the 20th century, he created masterpieces across numerous genres. His works include the March from *The Love for Three Oranges*, the suite *Lieutenant Kijé*, the ballet *Romeo and Juliet*, and *Peter and the Wolf*. Excluding juvenilia, he completed seven operas, seven [[Symphony|symphonies]], eight ballets, five piano concertos, and nine piano sonatas. After the Revolution of 1917 he lived in the United States, Germany, and [[Paris]] before returning to his homeland in 1936. In 1948 he was attacked for "anti-democratic formalism." The Nazi invasion of the USSR spurred him to compose an operatic version of *War and Peace*, his most ambitious work.

Russian composer, virtuoso pianist, and conductor, one of the last great representatives of Romanticism in Russian classical music. Widely considered one of the finest pianists of his day, he was influenced early on by [[Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky|Tchaikovsky]] and Rimsky-Korsakov, and wrote music marked by song-like melodicism and rich orchestral colors. He graduated from the Moscow Conservatory in 1892 and conducted the Bolshoi Theatre from 1904 to 1906. After a four-year depression that followed the disastrous premiere of his Symphony No. 1 in 1897, he completed his Piano Concerto No. 2 in 1901. After the [[Russian Revolution]] he left Russia permanently and settled in New York in 1918. Abroad he toured mainly as a pianist and completed just six works. He later moved to Beverly Hills, California.

American computer scientist and businessman, co-founder of [[Google]] with [[Larry Page]]. Born in [[Moscow]] to a Russian-Jewish family, Brin immigrated to the United States at age six. He earned a bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, then enrolled at [[Stanford University]] for a PhD. There he met Page and built a [[Search engine|web search engine]]. He left his doctoral studies to start Google in a garage in Menlo Park, California. He was president of [[Alphabet Inc.|Alphabet]] until 2019 and remains a co-founder and controlling shareholder. In 2023 he returned to contribute to [[Artificial intelligence|AI]] research.

Russian chemist and photographer known for pioneering work in color photography. He studied chemistry under [[Dmitri Mendeleev]] and became an expert in three-color photography. From around 1909 to 1915 he traveled the [[Russian Empire]] using a railway-car darkroom provided by Emperor [[Nicholas II]], recording its people, landscapes, and monuments in three-image color. Some of his negatives were lost, but most ended up in the [[Library of Congress]] after his death. His best-known work during his lifetime was a color portrait of [[Leo Tolstoy]]. Starting in 2000 the negatives were digitized and their color triples combined to produce hundreds of high-quality color images of Russia and its neighbors from over a century ago.

Individual who [[Murder|murders]] three or more people in separate events over a period of more than one month. The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] states that the motives of serial killers can include psychotic delusions, thrill-seeking, and attention seeking. Primary motivations usually involve psychological gratification, often sexual, though some killers lack motive altogether. The English term was popularized by former FBI agent Robert Ressler in the 1970s. It entered broader American usage in early 1981, when *The New York Times* used it to describe Atlanta serial killer Wayne Williams. The presence or absence of a significant break between murders, called the "cooling-off period," distinguishes a serial killer from a spree killer, though researchers have found the distinction of little value to law enforcement.

Professional [[Association football|association football]] league in Italy and the highest level of its football system. Established in the 1929–30 season, it restructured the Italian Football Championship, which had been played since 1898. It operates a promotion and relegation system with Serie B. Since 1924 the champion has worn the scudetto emblem on its kit the following season. Juventus, the most decorated club in Italy, is among its best-known teams, along with [[Inter Milan]] and [[AC Milan]]. As of 2024–25 the league ranked second in UEFA coefficient rankings, behind the [[Premier League]] in England and ahead of [[La Liga]] in Spain.

Monoamine [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]], also known as 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT). It regulates mood, appetite, and sleep in the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] and influences learning and memory. About 90% of the body's serotonin is synthesized in the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]], where it regulates intestinal movements. Platelets in the blood take up serotonin and release it during clotting. It is synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan. [[Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor|SSRIs]] and SNRIs, two classes of antidepressants, block its reabsorption to raise its levels. In [[Plant|plants]] and [[Insect|insect]] venom, it serves a defensive function by inducing pain.

Family of marine fish in the order [[Perciformes]]. The family once contained about 450 species in 65 genera, including sea basses and [[Grouper|groupers]], but taxonomic revisions split out Epinephelinae (groupers), Grammistini (soapfish), and Anthiadinae (anthias), leaving it much less speciose. Serranids are generally robust, with large mouths and several rows of sharp teeth, and many are brightly colored. All are carnivores, typically ambush predators that hide in cover on the reef. Many species are protogynous hermaphrodites, starting life as females and later changing to males. Representatives live in tropical and subtropical seas worldwide. A 2007 DNA study placed some former members with part of [[Scorpaeniformes]].

[[Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor|SSRI]] antidepressant sold under the brand name Zoloft, among others. It treats major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive–compulsive disorder]], panic disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, insomnia, and sexual dysfunction. It should not be used with monoamine oxidase inhibitors because of the risk of [[Serotonin|serotonin]] syndrome. Developed by scientists at Pfizer, it was approved for medical use in the United States in 1991 and is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines. In 2016 it was the most commonly prescribed psychotropic medication in the United States.

Slender, medium-sized wild [[Cat|cat]] native to sub-Saharan Africa. It has the longest legs of any cat relative to its body size, large ears, and a golden-yellow to buff coat spotted and striped with black. It stands 54–62 cm (21–24 in) tall at the shoulder and weighs about 9–18 kg (20–40 lb). A solitary carnivore active by day and night, it leaps over 2 m (6 ft 7 in) to pounce on prey, mainly [[Rodent|rodents]], with its forefeet. It inhabits [[Grassland|grasslands]], wetlands, moorlands, and bamboo thickets. Hunting it is either prohibited or regulated in range countries.

American educational children's television series combining live action, [[Animation|animation]], and [[Puppetry|puppetry]]. Created by Joan Ganz Cooney and Lloyd Morrisett, it was the first children's television show to use educational goals and a [[Curriculum|curriculum]] to shape its content, and the first whose educational effects were formally studied. It premiered on November 10, 1969, and has aired on [[PBS]] since its debut. It features [[Jim Henson|Jim Henson's]] Muppets. Its producers developed the CTW model, a system of planning, production, and evaluation based on collaboration among producers, writers, educators, and researchers. By 2006 independently produced co-productions were broadcast in 20 countries. As of 2022 the show had won 222 Emmy Awards and 11 [[Grammy Awards]], more than any other children's show.

Plant in the genus *Sesamum*, cultivated for its edible seeds. Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops known, domesticated well over 3,000 years ago. The cultivated species, *Sesamum indicum*, originated in India and was described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. Sesame tolerates drought and grows where other crops fail, and its seeds have one of the highest oil contents of any seed. World production in 2024 was 6.7 million tonnes (7.4 million short tons), led by India, Myanmar, and Sudan. Sesame was grown and pressed to extract oil at least 750 BC in the empire of [[Urartu]]. Most of its many wild relatives are native to [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]], and sesame allergies are common relative to other foods.

Japanese [[Zen]] monk and painter, considered a great master of Japanese ink painting. Born into the samurai Oda family, he trained as a monk at Shōkoku-ji temple in [[Kyoto]] and worked under the painter Tenshō Shūbun for about 20 years. In 1467 he traveled to China, then ruled by the [[Ming dynasty]], as a member of a Japanese envoy and spent three years studying Chinese landscapes and master paintings. The experience merged Japanese and Chinese styles into an individualistic style of Zen painting, with flattened perspective and emphatic lines. His works include landscapes, portraits, and birds and flowers. His acclaimed works include *Winter Landscape* (c. 1470s) and *Four Landscape Scrolls of the Seasons*. Many schools of art later claimed him as their founder.

Egyptian god of deserts, storms, disorder, violence, and foreigners. In the Osiris myth, Set murders and mutilates his brother [[Osiris]], but [[Isis]] reassembles the corpse and resurrects him long enough to conceive [[Horus]]. Horus then seeks revenge on Set, and many myths describe their conflicts. Set also had a positive role, accompanying [[Ra]] on his barque to repel Apep, the serpent of chaos. As lord of the Red Land, the desert, he balanced Horus's role as lord of the Black Land. Late in Egyptian history he is often depicted as a donkey or a man with a donkey's head.

Branch of mathematical logic that studies sets, collections of unique objects. Modern set theory was initiated by the German mathematicians [[Richard Dedekind]] and [[Georg Cantor]] in the 1870s, and Cantor is commonly considered its founder. Paradoxes in naive set theory, such as [[Russell's paradox]], led to axiomatic systems in the early 20th century, of which [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] (with or without the [[Axiom of choice|axiom of choice]]) is the best known. As a foundational system, set theory underpins the whole of mathematics and provides a framework for a mathematical theory of infinity. It has applications in [[Computer science|computer science]], philosophy, and formal semantics. Contemporary research ranges from the structure of the [[Real number|real number]] line to the consistency of large cardinals.

American animator, actor, filmmaker, and singer. He created and starred in *Family Guy* and *The Orville*, and co-created *American Dad!* and *The Cleveland Show*. He co-wrote, directed, and starred in the films *Ted* and *A Million Ways to Die in the West*. MacFarlane won five Primetime Emmy Awards for *Family Guy* and hosted the 85th Academy Awards in 2013. He has released ten studio albums in the vein of [[Frank Sinatra|Frank Sinatra]], beginning with *Music Is Better Than Words* (2011). He was executive producer of *Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey*, an update of the series hosted by [[Carl Sagan]].

Canadian actor, comedian, filmmaker, and [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] entrepreneur. Born and raised in [[Vancouver]], he moved to [[Los Angeles]] as a teenager to act in *Freaks and Geeks*. He often collaborated with writing partner Evan Goldberg and producer Judd Apatow, and starred in *Knocked Up*, *Superbad*, and *Pineapple Express*. He voices characters in the *Kung Fu Panda* series and other animated films. He co-developed the AMC series *Preacher* and executive produced *The Boys*. His Apple TV+ satirical comedy *The Studio*, which he created, wrote, and directed, earned him four Primetime Emmy Awards.

Inland sea of Japan separating [[Honshu]], [[Shikoku]], and [[Kyushu]], three of the four main islands. It serves as a waterway connecting the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] to the [[Sea of Japan]], and it connects to Osaka Bay, providing sea transport to the industrial centers of the Kansai region, including [[Osaka]] and [[Kobe]]. The sea is 450 km (280 mi) long from east to west, with an average depth of 38 m (125 ft). Almost 3,000 islands lie within it, the largest being Awaji-shima. Periodic red tides, caused by dense groupings of phytoplankton, kill large numbers of fish. Since the 1980s the sea's northern and southern shores have been linked by the Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project, including the Great Seto Bridge, which carries rail and road traffic.
